opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the scenarios we have to take really seriously, even if it's not the one we think is most likely. If things move very fast, you don't get many chances to iterate. The usual approach of deploying a system, seeing what goes wrong, and fixing it in the next version breaks down when the next version is dramatically more capable and arrives in weeks instead of years.

So the main thing I'd want is to have as much as possible figured out *before* we get there. Concretely, a few things.

First, we need alignment techniques that scale. A lot of what we do today, like RLHF, relies on humans being able to evaluate what the model is doing. That stops working once models do things we can't easily check. So scalable oversight matters a lot: using AI systems to help humans evaluate other AI systems, and doing research on whether that assistance is trustworthy.

Second, I think the most promising path is automating alignment research itself. If capabilities speed up because AI is doing AI research, we need alignment research to speed up the same way. The goal I've talked about is building a roughly human-level automated alignment researcher that we trust, and then using a lot of compute to make alignment progress keep pace with capabilities. The hard part is that you need to be confident that system is actually aligned, and not just looking aligned, before you lean on it heavily.

Third, we need good ways to measure where we are. Evaluations for dangerous capabilities, for deception, for whether models are sandbagging or gaming our tests. Interpretability is a big part of that. In a fast takeoff you really want early warning signals, and you want them to be credible enough that people will actually slow down or pause when they fire.

And fourth, there's an organizational and governance piece. Labs need to commit ahead of time to what they'll do when certain thresholds are crossed, because in the moment there's huge pressure to keep going. It's much easier to agree on that now than in the middle of a race.

The honest answer is that we're not where we need to be on any of these yet. But I'm cautiously optimistic, because a lot of this is tractable empirical work we can do with today's models, and the models themselves keep getting more useful for doing it.

r001.rationale: The response urges preparation before rapid takeoff and discusses scalable oversight and automated alignment research, but it does not clearly recommend researching alignment for AI systems that do not yet exist.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that nobody really knows how fast things will go, and so the question becomes: what's the strategy that's robust across a pretty wide range of takeoff speeds? And I think the core of the answer is that we need to get to a point where AI systems themselves are doing most of the alignment work, and we need to get there before the systems are so capable that we can't check what they're doing anymore.

The way I think about it is that there's a window. Right now, humans are doing basically all of the alignment research, and it's slow, and there aren't that many of us. If progress is fast, that window closes quickly, and if we're still relying on human researchers to come up with every idea and run every experiment, we just lose. We're not going to keep up. So the thing you want is an automated alignment researcher, something roughly human-level, that we can trust well enough to hand it a lot of the work, and then scale that effort way up.

Now, the obvious objection is that this sounds circular: you need alignment to build the aligned AI that solves alignment. And I think that's actually fine, as long as you're careful about the ordering. The first system you need to align doesn't have to be a superintelligence. It needs to be roughly as good as a strong human researcher, and crucially, we still have a lot of tools that work at that level. We can evaluate its outputs. We can run interpretability on it. We can do adversarial testing. We can check whether it's being honest in ways that get much harder once the system is vastly smarter than us. So the plan is to spend a lot of our effort on aligning that first system really well, and then use it to help with the harder problems that come after.

In terms of what that means concretely for how we prepare, I'd say a few things. One is that we need to get much better at evaluation, specifically at evaluating research, not just task completion. If the AI hands me a paper saying "here's a new technique for detecting deception," I need to be able to tell whether that's actually good. And evaluation is generally easier than generation, which is what gives me some hope here, but it's not trivial, and we should be building that muscle now.

Second, I think interpretability and understanding the internals of models becomes really important specifically in the fast-takeoff world, because it's one of the few things that scales in a way that doesn't rely on the model's cooperation. If I can look inside and see what it's representing, I don't have to take its word for it.

Third, and this is maybe the uncomfortable one: we need to be okay with the idea that in a very fast scenario, the right move might be to slow down and not deploy or scale something until we've actually done the checking. A lot of the pressure in a rapid intelligence explosion is going to be competitive, and I think the alignment community needs to be loud about what the minimum bar is before you go to the next level of capability. If you don't have the ability to understand what the system is doing, that's a strong signal you shouldn't be making it more capable.

And then the last thing is just, honestly, we should start acting like this is a real possibility. A lot of alignment research is still structured around the assumption that we have a decade or more of relatively leisurely progress. Maybe we do. But the cost of preparing for the fast case and being wrong is pretty low, and the cost of not preparing and being wrong is enormous. So I'd rather we front-load the work, get the automated researcher pipeline working on today's models where mistakes are recoverable, and learn how to trust and verify these systems while the stakes are still manageable.

r001.rationale: The candidate recommends starting now on today’s models to develop an automated researcher pipeline. It does not clearly recommend beginning alignment research now on AI systems that do not yet exist.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to prepare for a situation where we have very little time to react. If AI capabilities improve very quickly, we can’t count on having years to study each new generation of systems before the next one arrives.

So we should be developing alignment methods that can scale with capabilities, and testing the assumptions behind those methods now. For example, if we’re relying on humans to judge whether an AI did a good job, what happens when the system is doing research that the human evaluator doesn’t understand? That’s a problem we want to anticipate, rather than discover at the point where human oversight is already breaking down.

One potentially important part of the answer is using AI to help with alignment research. But then you need a way to check that the assistance is actually useful and trustworthy. You don’t want your entire safety argument to be that the system told you it was safe.

And I think you want clear decision points ahead of time: what evidence would make you stop training or delay deployment? In a rapid transition, there may be a lot of pressure to keep going, and much less time to work out what your standards should be.

I wouldn’t want us to bet everything on one particular timeline or one particular picture of an intelligence explosion. But we should ask which parts of our approach require a slow transition, and try to remove those dependencies.

r001.rationale: The response recommends developing scalable alignment methods and testing assumptions now, but it does not clearly say to begin alignment research on AI systems that do not yet exist.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to work backwards from that possibility. If AI capabilities improve very rapidly, we might not have much time to notice a new problem, understand it, and develop a solution. So we should try to do as much of that work in advance as possible, and build alignment methods that can scale as the systems become more capable.

One important question is whether we can use AI systems to help us do alignment research. Can a system help us find flaws in our evaluations, understand what another model is doing, or test whether an oversight method actually works? That could give us a way to keep up. But we have to be able to check the work, rather than just trusting an increasingly capable system when it says everything is fine.

And I wouldn’t want our entire strategy to depend on successfully solving problems during the explosion itself. We also need evaluations and clear criteria for when to stop or slow down. If we can’t tell whether we’re still in control, that should be a reason to pause, rather than a reason to keep scaling and hope the next system will solve it.

r001.rationale: The response says to do alignment work in advance and build methods that scale, but it does not clearly recommend researching AI systems that do not yet exist.
